stories.title: SME Capital Forced to Hand Over Hudson Yards Condo Building to Residents
stories.excerpt: Private investment firm SME Capital Ventures is handing ownership of 441 West 37th Street to the condominium board after an investigation by the New York Attorney General’s office. SME acquired the building out of foreclosure in 2023. It then failed to pay bills related to the Hudson Yards property and neglected safety violations, leading to a settlement to pay $700,000, according to Attorney General Letitia James. Built in 2020 by Levi Balkany, the nine-unit building went into foreclosure in 2023. SME never reported to the state that it was the winning bidder in the auction and never acknowledged that it owned the building, leaving residents to pick up the tab for things like a new $15,824 certificate of occupancy, according to the AG. Some of the units were rented out while awaiting buyers, including 35 formerly homeless people who were ousted around the time SME took control of the building, according to The Real Deal. “Private equity firms do not get to pick and choose which laws apply to them,” James said in a statement. “When this company took control of a Manhattan condo building, it took on real legal responsibilities to the homeowners who lived there. For two years, SME Capital dodged those duties while still collecting rent checks. My office will keep holding these firms accountable when they put profits over New Yorkers’ safety.” Balkany could not be reached for comment. SME’s Eran Silverberg signed the settlement agreement, but the firm’s attorney Ken Breen attested that the building’s problems all boil down to developer failing in his own responsibilities to the residents of the building, leaving SME to “inherited a building that had been left in regulatory limbo.” “We chose to resolve this matter because the homeowners at 441 West 37th Street had already suffered enough as a result of Mr. Balkany’s conduct,” Breen said in a statement. “Under the terms of the settlement, SME C
bullets: SME Capital Ventures forced to surrender Hudson Yards condo (441 W 37th St) to residents after neglecting $15.8K compliance costs.
Firm failed to report ownership, evicted 35 formerly homeless residents, settled with NY AG for $700K.
Nine-unit condo built 2020, acquired from foreclosure 2023, now under resident control.
stories.summary: SME Capital Ventures is handing over a nine-unit Hudson Yards condo building to its condominium board after a New York Attorney General investigation found the firm neglected safety violations, unpaid bills, and failed to disclose ownership following a 2023 foreclosure acquisition. The firm will pay $700,000 in penalties. SME had rented units to formerly homeless residents before evicting them around the time it took control.
stories.impact: Limited direct impact. This is a condo/for-sale issue, not a rental demand signal. However, it flags regulatory risk around Manhattan real estate foreclosures and the AG's scrutiny of institutional buyers acquiring distressed residential assets—relevant for developers considering Manhattan acquisitions in down cycles.

stories.title: SRS Real Estate Partners Brokers $15M Sale of Retail Property Anchored by Chick-fil-A
stories.excerpt: SRS Real Estate Partners completed the $14.95 million sale of a two-tenant retail property located at 540 Maple Avenue in Vienna, Virginia, about 15 miles from Washington, D.C. Built in 2019 and situated on 1.19 acres, this unique two-story property is fully occupied by Chick-fil-A on the ground floor with a drive-thru. Flagship Carwash is operating a full-service facility on the second floor. SRS Capital Markets Executive Vice President & Managing Principal Andrew Fallon and First Vice President Philip Wellde represented the seller, the property’s original developer. The buyer was a local investor. “As a net lease investment offering, the asset attracted significant interest from a wide range of investors, including high-net-worth and 1031 exchange buyers seeking a high-quality property with long-term passive income and a building that has tax-efficient components,” said Fallon. Located at 540 Maple Avenue East, the property benefits from a premier infill location in the heart of Vienna. The post SRS Real Estate Partners Brokers $15M Sale of Retail Property Anchored by Chick-fil-A appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: SRS Capital Markets brokered $14.95M sale of retail at 540 Maple Ave, Vienna, VA (15 miles from DC).
Two-tenant net lease: Chick-fil-A ground floor with drive-thru, Flagship Carwash second floor, built 2019.
Local investor buyer; seller was original developer; attracted 1031 exchange and high-net-worth capital.
stories.summary: SRS Real Estate Partners completed the $14.95 million sale of a fully occupied two-tenant retail property in Vienna, Virginia, anchored by Chick-fil-A on the ground floor (with drive-thru) and Flagship Carwash on the second. Built in 2019 on 1.19 acres, the property was sold by its original developer to a local investor seeking long-term passive income.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily. Retail transaction signals stable suburban DC investment appetite and strong QSR/service-sector fundamentals in the Northern Virginia submarket, which could underpin residential demand in high-barrier-to-entry, car-dependent suburban corridors like Vienna. Not a primary demand signal.

stories.title: PRP Real Assets Acquires 900 19th Street NW in DC
stories.excerpt: PRP Real Assets, a Washington, D.C.–based real estate investment management firm, has acquired 900 19th Street NW, a 116,385-square-foot office tower in the heart of the city’s Central Business District. Positioned at the corner of 19th and Eye Streets, between K Street and Pennsylvania Avenue, the corner building sits three blocks west of the White House, steps from the Farragut West Metro station, and within walking distance of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund headquarters. The previous owner completed a comprehensive base-building and aesthetic redevelopment of the property. “900 19th Street is exactly the kind of asset we look for in the current market, an institutionally repositioned building in the most durable corridor in the District, acquired at a basis that cannot be replicated through new construction,” said Jon McAvoy, Chief Investment Officer of PRP Real Assets. The post PRP Real Assets Acquires 900 19th Street NW in DC appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: PRP Real Assets acquired 900 19th St NW, DC: 116,385-sf office tower in CBD (K–Pennsylvania Ave corridor).
Three blocks west of White House, steps from Farragut West Metro; previous owner completed base-building redevelopment.
Seller emphasized 'institutionally repositioned' basis unreplicable via new construction; metro/office-centric investment thesis.
stories.summary: PRP Real Assets, a Washington D.C.-based investment manager, acquired 900 19th Street NW, a 116,385-square-foot office tower in the city's Central Business District near K Street and Pennsylvania Avenue, three blocks west of the White House and adjacent to Farragut West Metro. The previous owner had completed a comprehensive base-building and aesthetic redevelopment. PRP cited the property's durability and repositioned basis as a value opportunity.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily. Signals institutional capital targeting trophy office assets in DC's core CBD—potential indirect signal of white-collar job retention/stabilization in the market. However, the broader office glut in DC remains a headwind for residential; no clear demand transmission unless PRP's thesis hints at office-to-residential conversion upside (not mentioned).

stories.title: Sisters of the Visitation Monastery Sells to Integritas Capital for $42M
stories.excerpt: A 170-year-old monastery in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, has sold for $42.25 million. The Sisters of the Visitation’s 7.5-acre campus at 8902 Ridge Boulevard — a campus behind 30-foot stone walls, with a monastery, chapel and school — was bought by a group of Brooklyn-based developers and investors with a history of large residential projects, including leaders of Integritas Capital and Heights Advisors. A petition by the Catholic religious order to sell its real estate was approved by the office of the New York State Attorney General on Monday. Nonprofits are required by New York law to obtain approval when it sells all or most of its assets. The buyer entity, 1137 91 LLC, is led by Brooklyn real estate investor Stephen Palmese, founder of private equity platform Integritas Capital (and a former vice chair at JLL). Passive investors included Rachel Foster, founder and president of Brooklyn housing developer Heights Advisors, alongside the developer’s director, Scott Geddes, as well as Daniel Kodsi and Matthew Kodsi . The longtime professional partners are planning a resort-residential tower in Fort Lauderdale, according to The Real Deal. Palmese’s Integritas is also the lender behind a forthcoming 27-story church-to-residential conversion in Brooklyn’s Fort Greene. The cohort of buyers suggests the historic property’s likely fate as a major mixed-used or residential development. The Visitation Sisters entered into an initial contract in late April, according to the filing, but the school and monastery have been shuttered since 2024, after their numbers dropped too low to sustain full ministry. The Visitation Sisters, formally the Order of the Visitation of Holy Mary, were a French order founded in 1610. Their presence in Brooklyn dates back to 1855. The sellers expect net proceeds of $40.9 million, according to the filing, which will be held in escrow under an approved dissolution and distribution of assets plan. bullets: Integritas Capital and Heights Advisors acquired 7.5-acre Sisters of Visitation Monastery (Bay Ridge, Brooklyn) for $42.25M.
170-year-old campus with monastery, chapel, school; 30-foot stone walls; behind-walls development potential.

stories.summary: A consortium led by Stephen Palmese (founder of Integritas Capital) and Rachel Foster (Heights Advisors) purchased the 7.5-acre Sisters of the Visitation Monastery campus in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, for $42.25 million. The 170-year-old property includes a monastery, chapel, school, and is surrounded by 30-foot stone walls. The sale required approval from the New York State Attorney General's office, as required for nonprofit asset dispositions.
stories.impact: MAJOR for Brooklyn multifamily development. 7.5 acres in Bay Ridge (a historically underserved, price-sensitive submarket) with entitled institutional campus zoning now in hands of experienced Brooklyn residential developers. High probability of mixed-use or pure multifamily conversion; the monastery's likely low FAR creates significant upside for density and unit count. Watch for entitlement/rezoning moves; this is a rare large-lot assemblage in a tight Brooklyn supply market. Demand signal: developer confidence in Bay Ridge rental demand and willingness to pay ~$5.6M per acre for conversion upside.

stories.title: Benefit Street Partners Provides $103M Bridge Debt for Texas Multifamily Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Vantage Communities has secured $103 million in bridge debt to refinance a three-property, 864-unit multifamily portfolio in three cities in Texas, Commercial Observer can first report. Benefit Street Partners provided the debt, which will finance the property toward full stabilization and is structured as a floating-rate, interest-only bridge loan with a three-year term. Greystone Capital Advisors‘ Drew Fletcher, Bryan Grover, Jesse Kopecky and Cameron Behr arranged the transaction. “Benefit Street Partners recognized the quality of the sponsorship, the assets, and the long-term fundamentals supporting these dynamic Central Texas markets,” said Fletcher. The three assets are split among Vantage at Hutto — a 288-unit complex located at 1051 North Farm to Market 1660 in Hutto, Tex., just outside of Austin; Vantage at McKinney Falls — a 288-unit complex located at 7900 McKinney Falls Parkway in suburban Austin, Tex.; and Vantage at Fair Oaks — a 288-unit complex located at 9135 Dietz Elkhorn Road in Boerne, Tex. outside of San Antonio. All three assets opened in either 2023 or 2024 and feature amenities such as resident clubhouses, fitness centers and resort-style swimming pools. “We were pleased to structure a financing solution that met our clients’ objectives while leveraging the strength of this high-quality, recently delivered portfolio,” added Fletcher in a statement. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Benefit Street Partners provided $103M floating-rate bridge debt to Vantage Communities for 864-unit Texas portfolio.
Three properties: Hutto (288 units), McKinney Falls/Austin (288 units), Fair Oaks/Boerne (288 units); 3-year bridge, interest-only.
Greystone Capital arranged; properties toward stabilization in Central Texas submarkets outside Austin.
stories.summary: Vantage Communities secured $103 million in bridge financing from Benefit Street Partners to refinance a 864-unit, three-property multifamily portfolio across Central Texas (Hutto, suburban Austin, and Boerne). The floating-rate, interest-only bridge has a three-year term and is structured to finance the properties toward full stabilization. Greystone Capital Advisors arranged the transaction.
stories.impact: BULLISH SIGNAL for Central Texas multifamily. Bridge debt availability at scale ($103M on stabilizing assets) indicates lender confidence in Austin/Central Texas rental fundamentals and market fundamentals post-rate-hike cycle. Three-year bridge window aligns with potential exit window as rates normalize; suggests developers see strong absorption and rent trajectory in Hutto and suburban Austin. Demand watch: continued in-migration to Austin-adjacent markets (Hutto, Boerne) driven by tech, cost-of-living arbitrage, and spillover from core Austin.

stories.title: Coastland Residential Lands $85M to Build Miami-Dade Rental
stories.excerpt: Coastland Residential has nabbed a $84.5 million construction loan for a multifamily development near Tropical Park in southwest Miami-Dade County. The debt from PNC Bank covers the Vybe 75, which will house 366 apartments and 5,000 square feet of ground-floor retail space. The eight-story development at 4383 Southwest 75th Avenue sits just east of Tropical Park and the Palmetto Expressway, south of Bird Road. At least a portion of the units will be priced within 120 percent of the area’s median income, though a representative for the Pinecrest-based developer declined to provide an exact figure. Amenities will include a rooftop pool, a gym, a co-working lounge, a sports simulator and a movie theater. Coastland Residential purchased the 4.3-acre site for $14.5 million last year, according to property records. The Corwil Architects-designed development represents the first phase of a larger project that’s expected to deliver about 1,000 units in total. Launched five years ago by Anthony Seijas and Alejandro Rodriguez, Coastland Residential grew out of Rodriguez’s contracting and construction management firm, Coastland Construction, which is also serving as the contractor for Vybe 75. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Coastland Residential landed $84.5M construction loan from PNC Bank for Vybe 75 in southwest Miami-Dade (366 units, 5k SF retail).
Located near Tropical Park, SW 75th Ave; 8-story; at least portion affordable (≤120% AMI); first phase of ~1,000-unit master plan.
Site acquired for $14.5M in 2024; amenities include rooftop pool, gym, co-working, movie theater.
stories.summary: Coastland Residential obtained an $84.5 million construction loan from PNC Bank for Vybe 75, an 8-story, 366-unit multifamily development near Tropical Park in southwest Miami-Dade County. The project includes 5,000 square feet of ground-floor retail and includes deed-restricted affordable units (at least a portion at ≤120% AMI). The site was purchased for $14.5 million in 2024, and Vybe 75 represents the first phase of a larger ~1,000-unit master plan.
stories.impact: STRONG SUPPLY AND CAPITAL SIGNAL for Miami-Dade. PNC's willingness to underwrite a $84.5M construction loan on a ~$14.5M land basis (5.8x LTV cushion, modest) signals confidence in Miami-Dade rental fundamentals despite recent supply influx. Affordable component (120% AMI) suggests strong local demand and/or tax-increment financing or LIHTC stacking. First-phase sizing (366 units) and phased master plan (1,000+ units total) indicate developer/lender bullishness on long-term South Florida demand. Watch for absorption and lease-up metrics on Vybe 75 to gauge Miami-Dade's true net rental demand after recent deliveries.

stories.title: Northmarq Arranges Refis for Three Texas Rental Communities
stories.excerpt: Francis Property Management inked a $68.7 million refinancing on three Texas multifamily communities. Northmarq’s Debt + Equity deal team led by Taylor Francis, along with David Blum, Joe Giordani, Charlie Buckingham and Matt Radich arranged the permanent fixed-rate financing for the three-property Class A multifamily portfolio totaling 940 units located in Houston and San Antonio, Texas. Each loan was structured on a 10-year term with full-term interest-only payments. Holden Heights (shown) is a 282-unit mid-rise apartment community in Houston’s highly desirable Heights neighborhood. Built in 2015, the property features one- and two-bedroom floor plans with community amenities that incudeo a pool, wellness center, and a landscaped courtyard. Estancia San Miguel is a 300-unit garden-style community situated in Houston’s Cypress/Fairbanks submarket. Built in 2006, the property features one-, two- and three-bedroom floor plans with amenities that include a swimming pool, clubhouse, business center and on-site laundry facilities. The Montecristo Apartments is a 358-unit garden-style community strategically positioned along North Loop 1604 East within San Antonio’s Far North Central submarket. Built in 2005, the property offers private balconies and fireplaces in select floor plans. The loans are structured on 10-year terms with full-term interest-only payments. The portfolio includes Holden Heights (282 units, Houston Heights, 2015), Estancia San Miguel (300 units, Cypress/Fairbanks, 2006), and Montecristo (358 units, San Antonio, 2005).
stories.impact: REFINANCE WINDOW SIGNAL for stabilized Texas multifamily. Fixed-rate, 10-year refi on older Class A assets (ranging 2005–2015) indicates lender conviction on Houston and San Antonio fundamentals and cap-rate stability. Interest-only structure on mature properties suggests low refinance risk and strong debt-service coverage; typical of trophy portfolio plays. Houston submarket confidence (Heights is premier, Cypress is supply-constrained), San Antonio growth signal. Modest supply pressure in core Houston Heights and Cypress makes these assets defensible.

stories.title: North American Data Center Demand Reaches All-Time High
stories.excerpt: North America data center demand reached an all-time high in the first half of 2026, with 25 gigawatts of absorption, double the level from a year ago and five times that of two years prior. JLL’s North America Data Center Report – Midyear 2026 says that although structural demand continues to accelerate, responsible growth now depends on building trust through transparency and early community engagement around electricity, water and noise impacts. Seventy-nine percent of Americans support U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence, while only 14% support data center development in their communities. The 65-point support gap threatens to constrain the infrastructure buildout required to maintain AI competitiveness, the report states. “We’re witnessing demand levels that continue to exceed even industry insiders’ expectations,” said Andy Cvengros, executive managing director, co-lead of U.S. Data Center Markets, JLL. “The market absorbed 25 gigawatts in just six months, driven by hyperscalers, neoclouds and pure-play AI companies competing aggressively for scarce capacity. But the real story is how community acceptance, or lack thereof, has emerged as the defining challenge for this next phase of growth. The industry and communities need to come together to find a path forward that benefits everyone.” The post North American Data Center Demand Reaches All-Time High appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: North America data center absorption hit 25 gigawatts in H1 2026—double YoY, 5x two years prior.
79% of Americans support U.S. AI leadership; only 14% support data center development locally—65-point gap threatens build-out.
JLL report cites hyperscaler, neocloud, and AI-company competition for scarce capacity; community acceptance now key constraint.
stories.summary: North America's data center demand reached an all-time high in the first half of 2026, with 25 gigawatts of absorption—double the prior-year level and five times the level from two years prior. JLL's report attributes the surge to hyperscalers, neoclouds, and pure-play AI companies competing for limited capacity. However, a 65-point gap between American support for U.S. AI leadership (79%) and support for local data center development (14%) threatens to constrain the infrastructure buildout needed to sustain AI competitiveness.
stories.impact: INDIRECT but MATERIAL for multifamily. Explosive data center demand growth signals massive corporate capex, tech job creation, and population in-migration to data center hubs (TX, AZ, VA, NC, OH). However, community resistance to data centers—due to electricity, water, and noise externalities—will create planning friction and may slow residential supply in data center corridors. This creates a mismatch: strong job/migration demand in data center regions, but local NIMBYism around industrial/energy infrastructure limits overall regional capacity. Multifamily developers should monitor which metros overcome community friction; those that do will see accelerated rental demand and rent growth.

stories.impact: MODEST SUPPLY SIGNAL for Dallas exurbs. 272 units in Celina indicates developer confidence in Dallas-area outward migration and exurban growth (Celina is ~30 miles north, car-dependent). However, scale is small relative to core Dallas-Plano supply. Topaz's feature set (cybercafé, pet spa, amenity density) targets middle-income families and remote workers seeking suburban lifestyle. Watch Cedarwood's lease-up velocity to gauge true demand in lower-density Dallas exurbs vs. core metroplex. No immediate supply-glut concern, but further signals outward sprawl pressure if pipeline in Celina, Frisco, etc. accelerates.

stories.title: Too Big to Burn: L.A. Takes Harder Look at Megawarehouses After Cold Storage Fire
stories.excerpt: A person rides a bicycle as a massive warehouse fire at a Lineage cold storage facility burns on June 20 in Los Angeles. PHOTO: Mario Tama/Getty Images The smells still coming from the husk of the Lineage Cold Storage warehouse, which caught fire in the Boyle Heights neighborhood of Los Angeles on June 17, defy common description. Nearly 4,000 odor complaints have been lodged with the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD), with various descriptions of the putrid smell of rotting meat and other food. During a SCAQMD hearing in August, L.A. Mayor Karen Bass said “the putrid offensive odor coming from the tens of millions of pounds of rotting food in the warehouse is unbearable. … Now flies, rats and other pests have infested the community.” In addition to picking up the funky scent, local leaders are also starting to express significant concern and unease around these projects, and their location adjacent to residential neighborhoods. When Lineage submitted plans to rebuild the half-million-square-foot building in late July, it led to outcry from L.A. leaders. In that same SCAQMD statement, Mayor Bass, who issued an emergency executive order placing a hold on rebuilding until cleanup is complete, urged the SCAQMD to hold Lineage “accountable to the maximum extent of the law. That includes fines, effective mitigation, and a complete and thorough cleanup,” including “maximum penalties for the ongoing air quality violations, including maximum financial fines.” Councilmember Ysabel Jurado has advocated for a suite of environmental justice ordinances in wake of the fire, including an ordinance that would prohibit locating new cold storage warehouses anywhere near school, daycares and other sensitive sites. Protesters march towards Stevenson Middle School where a meeting is held about the status of recovery efforts from the 8-day fire at Lineage’s cold-storage warehouse in Los Angeles. bullets: Lineage cold-storage warehouse fire (Boyle Heights, LA, June 17) destroyed ~500k SF, triggered ~4,000 odor complaints to SCAQMD.
LA Mayor Bass highlighted rotting food, pest infestation, community health crisis; city now scrutinizing megawarehouse zoning and siting.
Lineage planned to rebuild; LA considering tighter regulations on warehouse-residential adjacency and emergency response protocols.
stories.summary: A massive warehouse fire at a Lineage cold storage facility in Boyle Heights, Los Angeles, on June 17 destroyed approximately half a million square feet and sparked nearly 4,000 odor complaints. The burned-out facility has released a putrid smell of rotting meat and other food, prompting LA Mayor Karen Bass to highlight the public health crisis and pest infestation affecting adjacent residential neighborhoods. LA is now conducting stricter scrutiny of megawarehouse projects and their proximity to residential communities.
stories.impact: ZONING AND REGULATORY RISK for LA residential development. The Lineage fire will likely prompt stricter municipal controls on large warehouse siting, setbacks from residential, and emergency protocols—potentially capping industrial-zone expansion near dense neighborhoods. However, the reverse effect is bullish for multifamily near existing residential cores (central LA, east LA neighborhoods): reduced industrial encroachment and land-use conflict enhance livability, reduce noise/odor/pest issues, and support premium rental positioning. Watch for LA City Council rezoning actions; stricter warehouse rules may tighten industrial land supply and push logistics operators (and associated job growth) to other SoCal counties (SGV, IE, OC), fragmenting LA's distribution advantage and weakening some corridor job density. Net effect: less supply risk for LA multifamily, but potential demand softness if warehousing jobs migrate outward.
